PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Park — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what parks are for — running, resting, tree meetings — and why the grass belongs to everyone.

What is this?

A park is a big green space that belongs to the whole town: grass for running, trees for shade, benches for resting, open from morning to evening.

What does it mean?

Shared green is the idea: no one owns the park, so everyone does — the town keeps it free on purpose, like a giant front lawn for everybody.

What does the child need to know?

You need running shoes, a ball or a kite or nothing at all, and a drink for the bench break. The tree provides the shade; you provide the visit.

Why this matters

Towns are full of hard, busy places — the park is the soft, slow one. Every person in town, every single day, is allowed to just... be in it.

What it teaches

Big-movement play (run, roll, climb), sensory noticing (bark, leaves, birdsong), sharing open space kindly, and the rarest preschool skill: doing nothing, happily, on a bench.

Words to learn

parkgrasstreeshadebenchlamppostpathpicnicfresh airseasons

Say this to your child

“"The park! Run the grass — fast, faster, flop! Meet the big tree — feel the bark, find the shade. Play the ball game, chase the pigeon politely... and rest on the bench. Ahh. The park is the town’s big green breath."”

Step by step

  1. Come in by the path — parks always have one, and it leads past everything.
  2. Run the grass: the soft field is the town’s biggest "yes" — run, roll, lie down, look at clouds.
  3. Meet the tree: bark by hand, leaves by shape, and the shade test — stand under it and feel the difference.
  4. Play your game — ball, kite, chase — and when the legs get heavy...
  5. The bench. The lamppost. The long slow breath. Parks end every visit the same way: sitting in the shade, being glad the town kept this.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one enormous tree does the heavy lifting over the bench and the lamppost — parks are measured by their shade, and this one has plenty.

Ask your child

"Who does the park belong to?" (everyone in town — nobody and everybody) "What does the big tree give us on a hot day?" (shade) "What do we do when our legs get heavy?" (rest on the bench)

What your child can say or do

Your child might adopt one tree with a name and a birthday, lie on the grass naming cloud animals until further notice, or treat the bench as the official finish line of every park visit, forever.

Out in the real world

Every US, UK and Canadian town keeps at least one park free for everyone, and the bench is the universal invitation to slow down. The tree on the card is decades old — parks are gifts from townsfolk long gone, kept for the townsfolk still coming.

Try it together

Meet-a-tree day: pick one tree, learn its bark by hand and its leaves by shape, and visit it every season — spring buds, summer shade, autumn colors, winter branches. One tree makes the whole park personal.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the park cost?" (nothing — it is free for everyone) "What do we do under the big tree?" (rest in the shade — the long slow breath)

This lesson pairs with the Park flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
